title: What is known about 1RB1LF_1RC1RF_0LD1RE_---1LC_0RB1RE_1LA0LE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LF_1RC1RF_0LD1RE_---1LC_0RB1RE_1LA0LE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape. Its right end is a doubling bouncer: a block of 10 pairs doubles at every sweep, paid for from a pool of 1s, and the tape is rewritten each time the pool runs out.
verdict: The question is open. At every right-end visit in state B the tape is [1^2 0 (10)^c] 1^a 0 (10)^b B>0. While a ≥ 2b + 3 the next visit is (a − 2b − 2, 2b + 2); otherwise the pool overflows and the tape is rewritten. Of all such configurations only the ones without the bracket and with a = 1 halt.

Why it has not halted. The doubling step keeps the parity of a, and a is even most of the time: in the first 109 steps there are 1,453 such visits and only 48 have a odd, in 7 short odd phases (pools 5, 61, 165, 165, 989, 1,853, 189 at their start). An odd phase that starts at (A, 0) halts only if A − 1 is one of the sparse values 2k+2 − 2k − 4, so the danger shrinks as the tape grows; a halt is possible but not expected.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 2,930 cells have been visited and 1,686 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The doubling step and where it can halt
claims.text: For T = 0^∞ [1^2 0 (10)^c] 1^a 0 (10)^b B>0 0^∞ (the bracket present or not): if a ≥ 2b + 3, the next right-end visit in state B is the same with (a − 2b − 2, 2b + 2). Among all these configurations (bracket absent or c ∈ {0, 1, 2, 5, 9}, 1 ≤ a < 40, b < 20) exactly those without bracket and with a = 1 halt. Checked against direct simulation, and on every doubling step of the first 3·10<sup>6</sup> steps of the run.

claims.title: Odd pools are rare
claims.text: In the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps the run makes 1,453 right-end visits of this form; a is odd at 48 of them, in 7 phases starting with a = 5, 61, 165, 165, 989, 1,853, 189 (at steps 28, 10,527, 212,888, 432,061, 43,052,524, 260,493,638, 262,189,033); a is never 1.

claims.title: A halt needs an exact hit
claims.text: Doubling from (A, 0) gives a = A − (2<sup>k+2</sup> − 2k − 4) after k steps, so an odd phase of this kind halts only if A is 3, 9, 23, 53, 115, 241, 495, 1005, …, about log<sub>2</sub> A values out of A. Odd phases are rare and their pools grow with the tape, so the chance that some future phase hits shrinks; nothing rules it out.

claims.title: The overflow rule
claims.text: The exceptional steps (a < 2b + 3) are not yet written as a formula; a complete macro machine would turn the parity bookkeeping into a proof strategy or find the halt.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows whether it halts. At the right end of the tape a block of pairs doubles at every sweep, paid for from a pool of 1s. The machine can only halt when that pool is down to a single 1 — but doubling always takes an even number of 1s, so with an even pool that can never happen. Only rare stretches with an odd pool are dangerous, and so far none of them has landed on 1.

facts.text: The doubling step, checked against simulation.
Visits with an odd pool in 10<sup>9</sup> steps.

sections.heading: Doubling, overflow, and a parity guard
html: Each time the head pushes the tape one cell further right in state B, the right part of the tape is a pool of 1s, a 0, and a block of 10 pairs: 1^a 0 (10)^b (sometimes with 1^2 0 (10)^c further left).
Doubling. If the pool is large enough, one sweep turns it into 1^(a−2b−2) 0 (10)^(2b+2): the pair block doubles and gains two, and the pool pays for it.
Overflow. When the pool cannot pay, the sweep runs into the 0s and pairs beyond and the tape is rearranged; a new, bigger pool appears and the doubling starts again from a small block.

The only way to halt is to have a pool of exactly one 1 with nothing to its left. Doubling always removes an even number of 1s, so an even pool stays even and is safe. In 109 steps the pool was odd only 48 times out of 1,453, in seven short stretches, and never reached 1. Starting from an odd pool A with an empty pair block, doubling reaches 1 only if A is one of 3, 9, 23, 53, 115, 241, 495, 1005, … — a thinner and thinner target as the tape grows.

explainer.title: A doubling bouncer guarded by parity

summary: A pool 1^a feeds a block (10)^b that doubles (+2) every sweep; overflows rewrite the tape. It halts only if a reaches 1 with nothing to its left; the doubling keeps a parity, so only rare odd-a phases are dangerous (7 in 10^9 steps, none hit).
